title: We Were Wrong About Swordfish
fullText: It's been given many names. Broadbill, Emperor, Gladiator. And while the ocean is full of predators all trying to brutally eat each other, the swordfish consistently remains at the very top. Their Latin name, Zifus Gladius, comes from the Latin and Greek words for sword, meaning its name is literally sword sword. And for thousands of years, we assumed that was exactly how it worked. It's got a 3-ft long sharpened sword attached to its face. So, it would only make sense that it would stab things with that sword. But recently, scientists have discovered that a swordfish that spends time stabbing its prey is actually the swordfish that's most likely to die. If you stab an animal, not only is your blade now stuck, but so is the rest of your face. And yet, somehow there's evidence of swordfish killing entire tuna. Barracuda, giant squids. Even worse, these swords aren't indestructible. They are bone. If a swordfish stabs a massive prey and that prey twists or dives, the sword can and will snap. And a swordfish without its sword is just a fish. A really bad fish with no hydrodnamics, balance, or defense. For millions of years, evolution has been sharpening a weapon that if used the way we thought it was used, would lead to certain death for the user. Which raises a massive question. If the sword isn't a sword, then what is it? Why would you bother attaching something so extravagant yet completely impractical to your face? And how have these creatures somehow still become apex predators? To find out what's actually happening, we have to look closer at what a swordfish even is. When most people see a fish with a long pointy nose, they immediately think marlin or sailfish. They lump them all together into a group called billfish. And while they do look similar on the surface, scientifically speaking, the swordfish isn't really related to them at all. Marlins and sailfish belong to the family is. But the swordfish is the one and only member of the family zyod. So how do they actually kill their prey? People assume they swim around stabbing their prey. It makes sense, right? You have a giant spike. You stab things with it. But they don't. If you spear a massive fish underwater, you are now physically tethered to a thrashing, panicked animal that weighs 100 lb. Your weapon is stuck. You lose all your speed. And in the open ocean, losing your speed is a death sentence. So, they whack it. They swim directly into a school of squid or mackerel at highway speeds. And they violently thrash their head from side to side, turning that rigid bill into a massive bluntforce bat and a razor sharp slashing blade. They aren't trying to stab the food like a kebab. They are trying to basically shatter it like a baseball bat. They break spines, [music] stun prey, and leave a trail of quite disabled victims in the water, which they can only then casually turn around and consume. Their sword isn't actually sharp like a knife, but it is still narrow. When they're moving at such high speeds, that much force on a still somewhat narrow edge will slash the fish open. It's like cutting a fish with something like a metal ruler. Swing it hard and fast enough and it will still slice. To eat these immobile or completely dead prey, you would expect something from an apex predator, like massive jaws and teeth. When a swordfish is born, that is exactly what it has. Baby swordfish are born with regular scales covering their bodies and a mouth completely full of sharp, aggressive teeth. But the second they reach adulthood, they lose all of them. Every single tooth falls out. Every single scale on their body disappears. Most animals in nature add weapons and armor as they grow up. But with swordfish, their sword is their teeth. Not that they're chomping with the sword, but that by cutting that fish with that sword is how they're able to cut the fish into smaller pieces and then swallow that hole. Scales create drag. So ditching those allows you to swing that sword faster, too, which means better diced up fish. Kind of cool. Except this still doesn't make any sense for how this strategy works. You don't see swinging as a strategy in basically any marine life because swinging doesn't really work underwater. Imagine trying to swing a bat in a pool versus the air. That creates an insane amount of drag, and you can't really hit anything hard, let alone fast enough to slice it. A swordfish should be snapping its own neck by trying to whip these fish that hard. Fortunately for swordfish, and unfortunately for everything else, most of the power is from their body and tail, not actually their neck. But the biggest reason isn't even really that or that their entire body is streamlined. It's really just because they're 1,000 lb. These are not really some sleek, graceful, elegant, skinny fish. They are beasts. Way bigger than you and way, way heavier, too. Being such a large size and having that much muscle is what allows you to be able to cut other fish just by simply being a beast. But keep in mind, swordfish aren't really like whales. Just because they got big doesn't mean they're designed to only eat plankton. They're clearly built for speed and aggression. So, what are they fighting? Well, only my favorite animal in the world, giant squid. I know on this channel I basically only mention sperm whales hunting giant squid, but swordfish actually do, too. They're a,000 lb, and giant squids are around 500, but even then, the fight isn't just one-sided the way it is with sperm whales. Swordfish will usually still have to target a smaller giant squid to be able to effectively hunt and kill it, and also ensure they don't leave with massive injuries. Giant squids live thousands of meters deep though, so they have quite an advantage in the fight. But fortunately, swordfish have a sword. When the squid reaches out to wrap its massive tentacles around the intruder, the swordfish violently whips its entire torso, transferring a,000 lbs of kinetic force straight into the sharp edges of the bill. They don't try to stab the squid's core. They systematically sever the weapons. They slash directly through the tentacles, completely disarming the massive squid in the dark. They use sheer brute force to physically amputate the squid's only means of defense and offense. Once the arms are gone, the squid is completely helpless. The swordfish just casually circles back, scoops up the severed tentacles, and consumes the rest of the disabled body. With a battle like this, though, swordfish could lose. Sperm whales are 50,000 lb. Giant squids are 500. That's like a 100 times weight difference versus a two times weight difference with a swordfish. You hear about the sperm whales more often because they can basically ensure they win over 95% of their encounters against giant squids. Swordfish have to be a bit more opportunistic. We still don't really have footage of these battles though because of how deep they are. So most of this is speculation from stuff like tentacle scars on the swordfish bodies. If you saw our video on the megalodon, you might remember how baby megalodons are born at over 6 ft starting from birth, making them already gigantic to start. This happens with most animals that give live birth under large marine predators. Swordfish don't do live birth though, which means they are barely a few millimeters long. They are entirely transparent and definitely don't have a giant sword. So, if they want to survive long enough to become 1,000 lb, they have to outgrow everything that wants to eat them, and they have to do it instantly. A swordfish grows faster than almost any other vertebrae on the planet. From the moment they hatch, their entire biological directive is just eating. They do eat tiny plankton to start, then tiny fish, then medium fish, scaling up their diet every single day until eventually they can eat giant squids. Get huge immediately or you die. Even at 4 years of age, they'll be essentially fully adult size, which is a lot faster than human development, especially considering we start somewhat large as babies. But this exact thing is what makes them basically mentally insane. When you're forced to grow that big and that fast, you have to be aggressive. You have to eat everything. Everything in the ocean is either food or it's in the way. There are verified, documented instances of swordfish attacking things that make absolutely no logical sense. They have charged and rammed deep sea submersibles thousands of feet below the surface. They have been recorded aggressively attacking massive multi-tonon oil drilling rigs. They have slammed into the holes of steelboats with so much force that they snap their own swords off in the metal. They will charge and ram solid steel at full speed. Most animals operate on a very, at least you could say, normal risk assessment system. If something is larger than you, made of metal, and making loud mechanical noises, you swim away from it. It's basic survival. The swordfish just completely ignores this. That aggression from birth makes it look like it's just always in a state of pure madness. If a submersible drops into their hunting ground with bright lights and loud thrusters, the swordfish is just angry. They will throw their thousand-lb bodies at industrial machinery purely out of territorial rage. They are so hardwired for absolute dominance that the concept of fear simply does not exist in their neutral pathways. Unfortunately, this kind of aggression means they live a more or less lonely life. If swordfish traveled in large groups, they would completely eradicate entire ecosystems in a matter of days. Outside of the brief moments of reproduction, you will almost never find adult swordfish traveling, hunting, or living anywhere near each other. They actively avoid their own kind. The ocean simply cannot support more than one of them in an area. If two adult swordfish decide to hunt in the exact same zone, they will drain that zone of life. There are not enough squid, not enough mackerel, and not enough energy in a single patch of the open ocean to fuel two of these guys at the same time. Even if they wanted to cooperate, their biology prevents it. If another swordfish is nearby, it is stealing your calories. It is threatening you. And considering swordfish feel threatened by a wall of steel, they won't take lightly to someone actually stealing their food. So, what actually kills them? Well, as I said, they're apex predators. Essentially, adult swordfish don't really get hunted. They don't get chased down by sharks, and they rarely ever fall victim to killer whales unless there's intentional coordination from a pod to stop it from fleeing. What does kill them are microscopic parasites or sheer exhaustion. The ocean is entirely filled with microscopic worms, parasitic copapods, and other nasty stuff. Swordfish are notorious for carrying massive loads of highly specialized parasites that latch onto their gills and feed directly off their internal organs. Because the swordfish is constantly burning thousands of calories to stay warm and swim fast, it exists on a pretty thin line. If parasites compromise their gills, their oxygen intake drops. If their oxygen drops, they can't swim fast. If they can't swim fast, they can't catch food. And then you die. Living in a constant state of hyperaggression, extreme temperature shifts, and massive caloric burn, also eventually degrades their bodies. Most swordfish, especially males, barely even live 10 years. Living like Larry, if Larry was a swordfish. Nature always balances the scales. And when you're this sick and awesome of an animal, it's going to cost you something. But at least you got to live a really sick, solo, wild life.
